input.question: How is Titan able to have an atmosphere pressure similar to Earth when it's gravity is so much lower than Earth's?
input.ground_truth: Cold makes sticky. Titan can hang on to so much atmosphere even though it’s gravity is much weaker, because the cold temperature means the collisions of gas particles are less energetic. Thus less likely to bounce hard enough that Titans gravity can’t recollect them.

Okay! Let’s imagine Titan is like a tiny, cold cousin of Earth.

Earth has a lot of gravity, which is like a big invisible hand that holds onto the air (the atmosphere) so it doesn’t fly away. Titan also has some gravity, but not as much as Earth. So you might think, “Oh, Titan should lose its air easily!” But here’s why it doesn’t:

Titan is very, very cold. Its air is mostly made of a gas called nitrogen, and it’s so cold that the air molecules move very, very slowly. When air molecules move slowly, they don’t have as much energy to escape into space. Also, Titan is big enough and has enough gravity to hold onto most of its air, even though it’s not as strong as Earth’s gravity.

So, even though Titan’s gravity is weaker than Earth’s, its cold temperature helps keep its air close, and that’s why it can have an atmosphere that is kind of similar in pressure to Earth’s, but not exactly the same.

Think of it like this: Imagine you have a balloon. If you let go of it on Earth, it flies away because the air pushes it. On Titan, the air is so heavy and slow (because it’s super cold), it’s like the balloon doesn’t want to go anywhere—it just stays close!
